title: What’s New in InfluxDB 3: 5 New Processing Engine Plugins
summary: The five most recent plugins from the InfluxDB team are live: Sagemaker, value counter, Chronos forecasting, simple data replicator, and a stock portfolio tracker.
body_text: Summary The five most recent plugins from the InfluxDB team are live: Sagemaker, value counter, Chronos forecasting, simple data replicator, and a stock portfolio tracker. Table of Contents The InfluxDB team has released five new Processing Engine plugins. They range from making it easy to call a hosted ML model to pulling in stock market data in real-time. Every one of them can be activated with a few terminal commands. No external services or tools—they all run inside your existing InfluxDB instance. Here’s what’s new, when you’d reach for them, and a few quickstart examples to get you going in minutes. Processing Engine primer If you aren’t familiar, the Processing Engine is an embedded Python runtime inside InfluxDB 3 that allows you to execute Python code on the following triggers: Schedule - Run code at scheduled intervals Data write - Runs whenever data is written to a table Request - A custom HTTP endpoint that handles incoming requests Plugins can query InfluxDB, transform your data, and write it back to a new table. They can also be used to hit external services outside InfluxDB. SageMaker inference The SageMaker plugin pulls rows of data, formats them how your SageMaker model expects, calls the model endpoint, and writes the prediction back to InfluxDB. It can build CSVs or 8 different JSON schema options, so it supports TensorFlow Serving, AWS’ built-in algorithms, and Hugging Face models. This plugin allows you to use your deployed SageMaker models without having to create a custom plugin. Just point the plugin at your endpoint to get anomaly scores, classifications, forecasts, or whatever else your endpoint returns, and have it written directly to InfluxDB. Example: Anomaly Scoring with Built-In AWS Model influxdb3 install package boto3 influxdb3 install package pandas influxdb3 create trigger \ --database iot \ --path "sagemaker.py" \ --trigger-spec "every:30s" \ --trigger-arguments 'endpoint_name=rcf-anomaly,source_measurement=metrics,feature_order={cpu}|{mem}|{rps}|{p99_ms},json_shape=instances_features,output_fields=anomaly_score=scores[*].score,interval=2min,limit=20' \ rcf_score With this setup, every 30 seconds the last 20 rows of metrics will get batched into a request to your Random Cut Forest endpoint. Each score comes back as a new row in the specified output table. Value counter This plugin is a port of the Telegraf value counter aggregator plugin. Point it at a field, and it will count how many times each unique value shows up in your data. It can be used with a data write trigger that counts as rows arrive or a scheduled trigger that aggregates the time window since it last ran. Common use cases for this plugin are HTTP status codes or log-level counts. Chronos forecasting The Chronos forecasting plugin allows you to use Amazon’s Chronos time series foundation models directly against your InfluxDB data. Chronos models don’t require a training step; you point the plugin at a measurement, and it returns a median forecast and prediction interval between 50% and 80%. This plugin works as a scheduled trigger for recurring forecasts and as an HTTP trigger for on-demand forecasting. The benefit of using Chronos models is that you don’t need to mess around with training data or tuning per series. If you want to start getting forecasts on your data as soon as possible, this is the fastest path. Example: On-Demand Forecast via HTTP influxdb3 install package chronos-forecasting influxdb3 install package torch influxdb3 create trigger \ --database mydb \ --path chronos_forecasting.py \ --trigger-spec "request:forecast_series" \ chronos_forecast_http influxdb3 enable trigger --database mydb chronos_forecast_http curl -X POST "http://localhost:8181/api/v3/engine/forecast_series" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"table": "sensor_data", "field": "temperature", "horizon": 28, "context_limit": 128}' This will return your historical context and a 28-step forecast, with each point having a median value and 50%-80% confidence bounds. Simple data replicator This plugin replicates data from your local InfluxDB 3 instance to a remote instance over HTTP, with built-in table/field filtering and renaming. It can be run on a schedule or on every data write. Data is buffered in a queue with automatic retries to support unreliable network connectivity. The data replicator makes it easier to set up edge-to-cloud deployments, sync dev and staging environments, or deploy InfluxDB in multiple regions. Example: Replicate Data on Every Write influxdb3 install package influxdb3-python influxdb3 create trigger \ --database mydb \ --trigger-spec "all_tables" \ --plugin-filename gh:influxdata/simple_data_replicator/simple_data_replicator.py \ --trigger-arguments host=example.com,remote_token=apiv3_token,database=remote_db,tables="home home2",unique_file_suffix=wxyz5678 \ simple_data_replicator_trigger influxdb3 enable trigger --database mydb simple_data_replicator_trigger Stock portfolio tracker With the stock portfolio tracker plugin, you can fetch live stock prices from Yahoo Finance. Define the tickers you want to track in a TOML configuration file and monitor values over time. This plugin is mostly an example of how versatile the Processing Engine is, showing how you can make external API calls, aggregate data on a schedule, and roll up your data. Mix and match your plugins These five plugins are just some of the most recent created by the InfluxDB team . The official plugin library already has plugins for data transformation, downsampling, anomaly detection, alerting, and more. The biggest benefit of the Processing Engine is the ability to combine these out-of-the box tools. Here is some inspiration: SageMaker Inference + Notifier - SageMaker writes anomaly scores to InfluxDB as time series data. You can then use the Notifier plugin to send alerts to Slack, email, or a webhook if a threshold is crossed without needing a separate alert stack. Value Counter + State Change - If you are tracking the status of something, you can use the value counter to tell you how many times a value has appeared and combine it with the state change to tell you when it changed. Together you can track frequency counts and status-change events for alerting, giving you a complementary view of the same data. Simple data replicator + Downsampler - Downsampling your data locally before sending it to your remote InfluxDB instance will help to reduce bandwidth usage. Simple data replicator + InfluxDB to Iceberg - This combination allows you to move hot data from InfluxDB to another instance for redundancy or regional access, and then export cold data to Iceberg for long-term storage. All five are live now in the influxdb3_plugins repository . Grab one, wire up a trigger, and see what you can build with the InfluxDB 3 Processing Engine. Related resources InfluxDB 3 download Official plugins Github repo Processing Engine docs InfluxDB 3 Explorer FAQs Q: Do I need to write Python to use these plugins? No, each plugin is ready to run after you install its dependencies with influxdb3 install package , then wire it up with influxdb3 create trigger . You only need to touch Python if you want to modify the plugin’s behavior or create a custom plugin. Q: Do I need to write Python to use these plugins? No, each plugin is ready to run after you install its dependencies with influxdb3 install package , then wire it up with influxdb3 create trigger . You only need to touch Python if you want to modify the plugin’s behavior or create a custom plugin. Q: Can I configure a plugin with a file instead of inline commands? Yes, every plugin supports using a TOML configuration file via the config_file_path argument. Using a configuration file is recommended for setups that require more than a few parameters. Q: Where do I see plugin errors or logs? Every plugin writes to the system.processing_engine_logs table in the trigger’s database. Q: Do these plugins work with all versions of InfluxDB 3? All five run on both InfluxDB 3 Core and InfluxDB 3 Enterprise; you just need the Processing Engine enabled ( --plugin-dir /path/to/plugins when you start the server).

title: SmartRent Earns Patent for ‘Brain’ of the Community Technology
body_text: Article Navigation Supporting proactive operations and automated response What earning a patent represents Continuing investment in multifamily technology Subscribe to our newsletter As multifamily communities become more connected, the infrastructure behind that connectivity matters more than ever. SmartRent has been awarded a utility patent for its multi-unit automation and control system, formally recognizing the architecture that enables coordinated device management across an entire community. This marks the company’s second utility patent and reinforces the strength of the platform that supports SmartRent solutions across multifamily housing. At the center of the patented design is a centralized system controller that acts as the “brain” of the community. Each housing unit includes a control hub that communicates with this central controller. The hubs facilitate communication between sensors and effectors — such as smart locks, thermostats and leak sensors — enabling coordinated monitoring and control across the property. Instead of managing disconnected devices or separate point systems, operators gain a coordinated architecture designed for community-level oversight. Supporting proactive operations and automated response The impact of this architecture is operational. Rather than discovering issues after damage has occurred, the system can detect events and initiate predefined responses. When a leak sensor is activated, for example, the system can automatically generate a corrective maintenance work order and provide limited digital access to maintenance personnel. These capabilities support faster response and more coordinated follow-through. Both management representatives and residents may access the centralized system controller through electronic devices such as smartphones. Residents can control effectors within their units, while operators maintain visibility and oversight across the community. This coordination between unit-level hubs and the centralized controller allows device activity to align more closely with operational workflows. What earning a patent represents Receiving a utility patent requires detailed documentation and technical review. SmartRent defined the system architecture, demonstrated how unit-level hubs communicate with a centralized controller and established how the design enables interoperability across a wide array of devices. The patent protects the core platform architecture that supports automated corrective maintenance and controlled access within multifamily housing. SmartRent product and engineering leaders Braeden Scheer, Vice President of Product Management; John Price, Senior Director of Research and Development; and Tyler Floyd, Director of Engineering are named inventors on the patent. Continuing investment in multifamily technology This patent builds on SmartRent’s broader intellectual property portfolio. In 2018, Smart Operations, previously SightPlan, was granted a utility patent (https://www.prweb.com/releases/sightplan-awarded-patent-for-innovations-in-real-estate-operations-and-service-management-863506481.html) covering innovations in task documentation, complex assignment routing, seasonal workflows and disaster preparedness. SmartRent’s hubs, which centralize control of multiple smart devices, are also protected by a design patent. Together, these patents protect architectural elements that support coordinated device management and automation within multifamily communities. For operators, that reflects continued investment in infrastructure purpose-built for multifamily communities, where multiple units, staff roles and device types must operate within one coordinated system. Smart for everyone.™

title: Best Client Portal Software for Law Firms in March 2026
summary: Compare the best client portal software for law firms in March 2026. MyCase, Clio, and Smokeball reviews with pricing, features, and security analysis.
body_text: You've probably looked at law firm client portal software before and walked away thinking the options either cost too much, require too much setup, or won't fit your firm's specific needs. MyCase and Clio dominate the market, Smokeball works well for certain practice areas, but none of them were built for how your firm actually operates. The challenge isn't finding a portal with features; it's finding one your clients will use, and your staff can manage without adding more administrative work. Here's what actually matters when you're comparing options in March 2026. TLDR: MyCase, Clio, and Smokeball bundle client portals into practice management systems starting at $39-$89/month. Secure portals with encryption and role-based access save law firms 1-5 hours weekly on status update requests. Mobile apps drive 80% client adoption, while browser-only portals see low engagement rates. Watch for hidden costs: storage limits, payment processing fees (2.5-3.5%), and premium security features. Stacker lets you build custom client portals with AI and no-code tools when legal software doesn't fit your workflow. What Is Client Portal Software for Law Firms Client portal software for law firms is a secure, web-based system that gives your clients access to their case information, documents, and communication history in a single central location. Instead of juggling email threads, phone calls, and physical file requests, clients log in to view updates, upload documents, and message your team directly. A client portal creates a single source of truth. Your case files, invoices, appointments, and messages live in one place where both your team and clients can access them securely. Clients get transparency into their matters without constant back-and-forth, while your staff reclaims time previously spent on routine status updates and file retrieval. Why Law Firms Need Client Portal Software in 2026 Client expectations have shifted. Today's legal clients want the same digital access they get from their bank or healthcare provider: the ability to check case status at 10 PM on a Sunday, not wait until business hours to call your office. According to the American Bar Association's 2023 Websites & Marketing TechReport, only 35% of law firms offer a secure client portal. The value shows up in reduced interruptions. When clients log in to check case status or download documents themselves, your staff fields fewer routine requests and spends less time on repetitive communication. Client satisfaction improves when people feel informed without requiring manual updates from your team. Key Features to Look for in Law Firm Client Portals Not all client portals are equal. When comparing different platforms, focus on the features that protect your firm and save your team time. Security should be non-negotiable. Look for end-to-end encryption, multi-factor authentication, and role-based permissions that let you control exactly what each client sees. You need granular access controls so clients only view their own matters, not other cases in your system. Document management separates adequate portals from good ones. Your portal should handle version control, allow clients to upload files directly, and let you organize documents by matter type or case stage. Stacker (Best Overall) Stacker is a no-code tool that lets law firms build custom client portals and internal dashboards on top of their own data, instead of adapting to a fixed practice-management layout. You design the data model, client views, and permissions so the portal matches your exact intake, matter stages, and communication patterns. What they offer: AI-assisted app builder that creates a working portal from a plain-language description, then lets you refine it in a visual editor. Built-in relational data layer plus live connections to Airtable, Google Sheets, and other sources, so you can pull from existing case or client records. Role-based permissions and field-level access controls so clients see only their own matters, while attorneys and staff get full or scoped internal views. Good for: Firms with specialized workflows or multi-practice setups that need a portal tailored to their processes, including custom intake flows, matter views, and vendor or partner access. Limitation: Stacker is not a full practice-management suite (dockets, a full billing engine, etc.), so it works best when paired with existing systems or used as a custom front-end over your current data. Bottom line: Stacker is the best option when your firm needs a portal that fits how you already work, with AI-assisted development, flexible data structures, and granular permissions, without hiring developers. MyCase MyCase is a practice management system for small to mid-sized firms that includes a built-in client portal tied directly to case files, billing, and scheduling. Clients log in via a dedicated page to view updates that mirror the attorney-facing system in a simpler format. What they offer: Integrated portal for documents, invoices, appointments, and case updates tied to MyCase matters. Secure messaging between clients and firm staff within the same environment. Mobile apps for iOS and Android so clients can access their portal on phones. Good for: Firms that want an all-in-one practice management tool with a straightforward client portal and do not need heavy customization beyond basic branding. Limitation: Portal layouts and workflows are tightly coupled to MyCase’s internal structure, which makes it harder to tailor the experience to specialized or non-standard practice workflows. Bottom line: MyCase is a solid choice when you want practice management and a simple, bundled portal in one subscription and are comfortable working largely within its defaults. Clio Clio is a leading cloud practice management product that includes a client portal inside Clio Manage, with a strong focus on client experience, integrations, and mobile access. Clients receive invitations from their attorney, set their own password, and can use a browser or the Clio for Clients app. What they offer: Portal access to shared documents, invoices, appointments, and case updates. Secure messaging threads are attached to matters, keeping communication in one place. Native client mobile app (iOS and Android) with push notifications for new activity. Good for: Firms that care about client experience, rely on integrations, and prefer a mature practice management environment with an integrated portal. Limitation: Customization of the client-facing experience is moderate, and pricing can feel high for smaller firms that mainly want portal capabilities without Clio’s broader feature set. Bottom line: Clio is a strong fit for firms that will use its full practice stack and want a polished, app-based portal, less so for teams that only need a highly tailored portal layer. Smokeball Smokeball is case management software with an embedded client portal, designed especially for firms in areas such as family law and personal injury. Its portal focuses on visual case timelines and automation-driven updates tied to internal workflows. What they offer: Client-facing case timelines that show milestones, key dates, and upcoming tasks. Document sharing with a dedicated client view, where you control which files appear. Sync internal case management workflows with the client portal to reduce manual status updates. Good for: Firms in practice areas like family law or personal injury that want a visual timeline view for clients and a tight linkage between internal matter tasks and portal updates. Limitation: Portal customization options are limited compared to standalone client-communication tools, and the experience is closely tied to Smokeball’s internal structures and supported practice types. Bottom line: Smokeball works well when your practice area aligns with its strengths, and you want clients to see a timeline-style case progress, but it is less flexible for firms with very different workflows or branding needs. Side-by-Side Comparison of Law Firm Client Portal Options Feature Stacker MyCase Clio Mobile App Mobile-responsive web portal Yes (iOS/Android) Yes (iOS/Android) Secure Messaging Yes (configurable in-app messaging) Yes Yes Document Sharing Yes, with structured client views Unlimited with version control Unlimited with version control Payment Processing Via integrations (optional setup) 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction Best For Firms needing custom workflows and portals without developers Small to mid-size firms across practice areas Firms focused on client experience and integrations Setup Time Days for a tailored portal (hours for a basic build) Minutes per client Minutes per client Client Portal Customization High: data model, layouts, and permissions defined by you Basic branding options Moderate branding and layout options Common Client Portal Implementation Challenges Client adoption often determines whether a portal succeeds or fails. According to the 2025 Legal Client Experience Report, firms using self-service mobile apps achieve 80% adoption and save an average of 1,329 hours per year. Traditional browser-based portals experience low engagement when clients forget their login details or find the interfaces unintuitive. Data migration from existing systems needs careful planning. Map your current data structure first, then move historical case files, client records, and billing information in phases instead of all at once to reduce the risk of data loss. Security and Compliance Considerations for Legal Client Portals Attorney-client privilege collapses if your portal leaks data. State bar ethics rules require lawyers to protect client information, making security a professional responsibility. Your portal needs AES-256 encryption for stored data and TLS 1.2 or higher for transmission. Request written confirmation of encryption standards from vendors before contracts. GDPR affects firms serving EU clients, requiring explicit consent for data processing and the ability to delete data. California's CCPA and similar state laws create parallel obligations domestically. Audit trails log every action: document access, file downloads, and case record changes. These records matter during breach investigations or malpractice claims. Build breach response procedures now. Define notification contacts, client communication timelines, and state bar disclosure requirements. Preparation reduces crisis chaos. How Client Portals Reduce Administrative Workload Client portals cut administrative time by removing repetitive status update calls and email exchanges. When clients log in to check case progress themselves, your staff no longer has to field routine "what's happening with my case" requests that consume hours each week. According to MyCase's 2024 Legal Industry Trends Report, secure text messaging tools saved 44% of law firms one to two hours weekly, with 17% saving three to five hours. Portal messaging creates the same time savings by moving client communication into a structured system where conversations stay attached to case files. Document version control problems disappear. Instead of emailing attachments back and forth, clients upload files directly, so your team can access the latest version. Mobile Access and Client Portal Apps Clients check case status from their phones, not desktop computers. Your portal needs to work on mobile devices or clients won't use it. The question is whether you need a dedicated mobile app or whether responsive web design works. Native apps like the Clio for clients app and MyCase client portal app offer smartphone features, including push notifications for case updates and document uploads through phone cameras. Clients download these from app stores and get alerts when your firm shares new documents or messages. Responsive web portals work through mobile browsers without requiring downloads. Clients access the same portal URL from any device, and the interface adapts to screen size. This approach skips app store approvals and works across all devices. Test mobile access yourself before rolling out to clients. Try uploading a photo from your phone, checking case status remotely, and sending a message through the mobile interface. Building Custom Client Portals With No-Code Solutions No-code tools let you build client portals that match your exact requirements. You define the data fields, design the client-facing interface, and set permissions that control what each user sees. Building custom solutions solves integration problems by creating a unified client portal that pulls from your existing tools, whether that's case management, billing, or document storage, without maintaining separate systems. How Stacker Helps Law Firms Build Custom Client Portals Law firms with specialized workflows often run into limitations with generic legal software. Stacker lets you build custom client portals that match your exact requirements without developers. The AI app builder generates a working portal from your description. Customize through a visual editor: design intake forms, set up case dashboards, and create document libraries organized by practice area. Role-based permissions control access at granular levels. Clients see only their matters, while attorneys view full case details and staff access specific workflow stages. Stacker connects to existing data sources, whether spreadsheets tracking cases or databases holding client records. Changes sync in real time. Automate notifications when case statuses change or new documents are uploaded. Final Thoughts on Choosing Client Portal Software The right law firm client portal software cuts administrative work and keeps clients informed without constant manual updates from your team. Security and mobile access matter more than flashy features you won't use. Pick a portal that matches your workflow, test it with a small group of clients first, and watch how much time you reclaim each week. If you want to see what a tailored portal could look like for your firm, try Stacker for free and build a first version without involving developers. FAQs How do I get clients to actually use a law firm portal? Roll out your portal with a clear onboarding email that explains what clients can do (check case status, upload documents, message your team) and includes their login credentials. Follow up with a brief tutorial during your next client meeting, and clients using mobile apps see 80% adoption rates compared to browser-only portals. What security features are required for attorney-client privilege protection? Your portal needs AES-256 encryption for stored data, TLS 1.2 or higher for transmission, multi-factor authentication, and role-based permissions that restrict clients to viewing only their own matters. Request written confirmation of these encryption standards from vendors before signing contracts. Can I build a custom client portal without hiring developers? Yes, no-code tools like Stacker let you build portals tailored to your firm's workflow through visual editors and AI builders. You design intake forms, set up case dashboards, control granular permissions, and connect to existing data sources without writing code. How much time does a client portal save law firms? Firms using self-service portals save an average of 1,329 hours annually by reducing routine status-update calls and document-retrieval requests. When clients check case progress themselves, your staff no longer has to field repetitive inquiries that consume hours each week. What's the difference between MyCase and Clio client portals? Both offer document sharing, secure messaging, and case updates as part of their practice management systems. MyCase and Clio function similarly for basic portal needs, with the main differences appearing in their broader case management features, mobile app interfaces, and pricing structures instead of portal-specific capabilities.

title: SCE Marks 140 Years of Innovation
summary: Imagine a world where turning the lights on with a flip of a switch wasn't an option. Before July 4, 1886, that was the reality. On that day, electric lights illuminated ...
body_text: Imagine a world where turning the lights on with a flip of a switch wasn’t an option. Before July 4, 1886, that was the reality. On that day, electric lights illuminated Visalia’s Independence Day celebration for the first time, kicking off a 140-year legacy of innovation that now powers over 15 million people across Southern California. SCE continues to build on its 140-year legacy of innovation, safely delivering reliable, clean and affordable electricity to millions. The evolution of electricity in Southern California : July 4, 1886: Holt and Knupps — later becoming Visalia Electric Light and Gas Company — use a steam engine to power arc lights so town festivities could commence on the evening of July 4, 1886. 1896-1899: Southern California Edison is born through the merging of numerous local power companies, driving innovation with the powering of electric trolley cars, building hydroelectric facilities and adopting three-wire conduit technology to minimize power line clutter. 1902-1950: SCE brings transmission lines to Los Angeles and neighboring communities. Steam, electric and hydroelectric facilities help strengthen California's agricultural industry. 1968-1984: Three nuclear units are built at the San Onofre Nuclear Generating Station , generating roughly 4,850 megawatts of power. 1980: SCE announces a commitment to renewable and alternative power , using wind, solar, geothermal, fuel cells, hydroelectricity and combined heat and power. 1989-1996: SCEcorp — SCE's parent company — is renamed Edison International and expands globally with the opening of its subsidiary, Edison Mission Energy, in London. Operations later expanded to Australia. 2000-2016: SCE increases rooftop solar generation for residents, invests in and expands wind power generation infrastructure, and upgrades 5 million meters with smart meter technology. 2017: SCE launches " Energy for What's Ahead ,” placing clean power , electrification and wildfire mitigation as the top priorities. 2018-2026: SCE reimagines the grid to reduce greenhouse gases, leads the electrification of transportation infrastructure, increases reliability and addresses climate risks — all in support of California's goal to reach of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2045 while also meeting rising demand for electricity. For more information on SCE’s history, click here .

title: Web Application Builder: The Ultimate 2026 Guide & Tips
summary: Learn what a web application builder is, key features, security, and how to choose the right platform. Get no-code tips and pro insights to start building.
body_text: Web application development has come a long way from the days of needing a computer science degree to build anything. A modern web application builder is a platform that lets you create web based applications with minimal manual coding, making powerful, custom software more accessible than ever. These platforms, especially no code tools, let you build visually, turning complex ideas into functional products without writing endless lines of code. This guide will walk you through everything you need to know. We will cover what a web application builder is, its key features, and the technical concepts behind the scenes. By the end, you’ll be able to choose the right tool for your project and understand the lingo like a pro. Quick verdict: What Kind of Web Application Builder Do You Need? The right web application builder depends on what you are building. If you need a simple website, landing page, or portfolio, a website builder may be enough. If you need an internal tool, dashboard, approval workflow, or admin panel, choose a builder that supports data connections, user roles, and business logic. If you need a SaaS product, customer portal, marketplace, directory, or production-grade business application, choose a web application builder with frontend flexibility, backend integrations, authentication, scalability, and a clear path beyond the prototype stage. That is where a platform like WeWeb fits: it gives teams a visual way to build custom web apps while keeping the flexibility to connect to scalable backends , APIs, and databases. Builder type Best for Typical limitations When to choose it Website builder Marketing sites, landing pages, portfolios, blogs, and simple content pages. Limited support for complex app logic, user roles, dynamic workflows, and backend-connected product experiences. Choose this when your main goal is publishing content, not building interactive software. Internal tool builder Admin panels, dashboards, CRUD tools, approval workflows, and operational tools for employees. Often less suited for polished customer-facing apps, custom UX, SaaS dashboards, or branded portals. Choose this when the app is mainly for internal teams and speed matters more than custom frontend design. Web application builder SaaS products, customer portals, marketplaces, directories, internal tools, and custom business applications. Requires more planning around data, authentication, permissions, scalability, and integrations. Choose this when you need a real interactive product with users, data, workflows, and room to scale. What is a Web Application Builder, Anyway? A web application builder is a platform that lets you create web based applications with minimal manual coding. It provides a visual interface, often with drag and drop functionality, and a library of pre built components. This means even non developers can assemble everything from internal tools and customer portals to full fledged SaaS products. These builders exist on a spectrum from low code (requiring some scripting) to no code (requiring zero programming). The no code movement is rapidly changing how software is made. In fact, by 2025, an estimated 70% of new applications are projected to be built using low code or no code technologies, a huge jump from less than 25% in 2020. This shift empowers founders, agencies, and enterprise teams to build and launch products faster than ever before. A modern web application builder like WeWeb combines AI with no code , allowing you to generate a complete application from a simple text prompt in minutes. Key Features to Look For in a Web Application Builder When you’re evaluating a web application builder, certain features are essential for a smooth and powerful experience. Here are the core capabilities you should look for: Visual Editor & Drag and Drop Design: This is the heart of a visual builder. It lets you design your app’s user interface by dragging elements like buttons, forms, and tables onto a canvas, giving you an intuitive way to control layout and style without touching HTML or CSS. Ready Made Templates and Components: Good platforms provide pre designed templates for common applications (like dashboards or client portals) and a library of reusable components. This accelerates development and ensures your app follows UI and UX best practices from the start. Integration Options (APIs and Plugins): An application rarely lives in a vacuum. A critical feature is the ability to connect to external services. Look for built in connectors for things like payment gateways, CRMs, or the ability to make custom REST API calls. This extensibility is what allows you to build real world, data driven apps. Security and Scalability Built in: A professional grade web application builder handles security and scalability for you. This includes user authentication, data protection, and the ability to handle a growing number of users without performance issues. You can focus on your app’s features, knowing the underlying infrastructure is solid. One Click Deployment and Hosting: Once your app is ready, the platform should simplify the deployment process. Many offer one click publishing, which packages your app and deploys it to the cloud automatically. This removes the headache of managing servers and lets you get your product in front of users instantly. A Closer Look: Technical Concepts in Web App Development While no code builders hide the complexity, understanding a few technical concepts can be helpful, especially if you’re working with more advanced tools or frameworks like ASP.NET Core. Understanding Minimal APIs and the WebApplicationBuilder In the .NET world, the term Minimal API WebApplicationBuilder refers to a streamlined approach for building web APIs, introduced in .NET 6. Traditionally, setting up an API required a lot of boilerplate code. Minimal APIs simplify this. The WebApplicationBuilder is an object that lets developers configure services, define API endpoints, and launch a web server with just a few lines of code, making it perfect for building microservices and simple endpoints quickly. Working with Ports in Your Application When you run a web app locally, it “listens” for requests on a specific network port. Think of a port as a numbered channel on your computer’s IP address. By default, browsers use port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS. Development servers often use other ports, like 5000 or 8080. You might need to change a port to avoid conflicts when running multiple apps or to use standard ports in a production environment. Listening on All Interfaces (0.0.0.0 vs. localhost) By default, many development servers listen on localhost , which means the app is only accessible from your own machine. If you want to access it from another device on your network, you need to configure it to “listen on all interfaces”. This is often done by binding the server to the IP address 0.0.0.0 . It’s a simple change, but it’s crucial for testing on mobile devices or sharing a development preview with a colleague. Just be mindful of security and use a firewall to control access when exposing your app to a network. Why HTTPS Configuration is Non Negotiable HTTPS configuration is the process of setting up your web app to use an encrypted connection. This is essential for protecting data and building user trust. Browsers like Google Chrome now mark all HTTP pages as “Not Secure”, which can scare users away. Furthermore, using HTTPS is a factor in search engine rankings, and many modern browser features only work on secure connections. Today, over 88% of websites use HTTPS by default. Any serious web application builder should provide and enforce HTTPS for all deployed apps. Managing Your App’s Behavior: Configuration, Logging, and Dependencies These three concepts are the bedrock of any well architected application, ensuring it’s flexible, maintainable, and easy to debug. The Role of Configuration in Web Development Configuration refers to all the settings that control how your application behaves without changing its code. This includes things like database connection strings, API keys, and feature flags. By separating configuration from code, you can deploy the same application in different environments (like development and production) just by changing the settings. What is Logging and Why It’s Your Best Friend Logging is the process of recording events that happen while your application is running. Think of it as your app’s diary. It writes down informational messages, warnings, and critical errors. When something goes wrong, logs are the first place you look to diagnose the problem. Without good logging, you’re essentially flying blind. Good logs are also crucial for security audits; compliance standards like PCI DSS for credit cards require detailed logging to track access to sensitive data. Demystifying Dependency Injection Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern that helps you write more modular and testable code. Instead of a component creating its own dependencies (like a database connection), those dependencies are “injected” from an outside source. This “inversion of control” makes your components loosely coupled, meaning you can easily swap out implementations. For example, you can inject a mock database for testing without changing the component’s code. Many modern frameworks have dependency injection built in. What is Environment Configuration? Environment configuration is the practice of tailoring your app’s settings for the specific environment it’s running in, such as development, testing, or production. For example, in development, you might use a local test database, while in production, you connect to a powerful, secure cloud database. This allows the same code to work everywhere, with only the configuration changing. It’s a fundamental practice for professional software deployment. Web App vs. Progressive Web App (PWA): What’s the Difference? All PWAs are web apps, but not all web apps are PWAs. A standard web app runs in a browser and typically requires an internet connection. A Progressive Web App (PWA) is a web app that has been enhanced with modern browser features to behave more like a native mobile app. Key differences include: Offline Capability: PWAs use “service workers” to cache content, allowing them to work even when the user is offline. Installability: Users can “install” a PWA to their device’s home screen, allowing it to launch in a standalone window just like a native app. App like Features: PWAs can deliver push notifications, which helps with user engagement. Companies that have adopted PWAs have seen impressive results. For instance, AliExpress increased conversion rates for new users by 104% after launching their PWA, largely because it provided a faster, more reliable experience. How to Choose the Best No Code Web App Builder for You The “best” no code web app builder really depends on your project’s specific needs. Here are the key criteria to consider when making your choice. Use Case Fit: Some builders excel at creating internal tools from spreadsheets, while others are designed for complex, scalable SaaS products. Match the platform’s strengths to your goal. Learning Curve: How intuitive is the platform? If you’re a non technical founder, you’ll want a tool with great documentation and a gentle learning curve. Flexibility and Extensibility: What happens when you hit a wall? The best platforms don’t lock you in. A builder like WeWeb stands out because it allows you to import custom code components. This means if a feature isn’t available out of the box, a developer can build it for you, giving you the best of both no code speed and custom code power. Performance and Scalability: Ensure the platform can handle your expected user load and data volume. Look for options that allow you to connect to scalable backends or even self host your application for full control. Integration Capabilities: Your app will likely need to talk to other services. Check for a robust library of built in integrations or, at a minimum, the ability to make custom API calls. Security and Compliance: If you’re handling sensitive data, make sure the platform meets industry security standards and offers features like role based permissions and data encryption. Vendor Lock in: Can you export your code or data if you decide to leave the platform? A web application builder that allows you to self host your final application, like WeWeb, gives you true ownership and freedom, protecting you from future platform changes or pricing hikes. Cost: Analyze the pricing model. Is it based on users, usage, or a flat fee? Project your costs as you scale to avoid surprises. By carefully evaluating these factors, you can find a web application builder that not only meets your needs today but also grows with your vision. Why teams choose WeWeb as their web application builder A web application builder should help you launch quickly, but it should not trap you in a basic prototype. If you are building a serious web app, you need more than drag-and-drop design. You need frontend flexibility, backend freedom, authentication, integrations, performance, and a path to scale. WeWeb is built for teams that want the speed of visual development without giving up control over the final product. You can design your frontend visually, connect to your backend or APIs (or use WeWeb's native backend), manage authentication and user roles, build dynamic pages, and launch production-grade applications from one platform. WeWeb is especially useful for: SaaS products Customer portals Internal tools Marketplaces and directories Admin panels and dashboards AI-powered applications Enterprise business apps Unlike website builders that focus on static pages, WeWeb is designed for interactive, data-driven applications. And unlike many internal tool builders, it gives you pixel-perfect control needed to build polished customer-facing experiences. If your goal is to build something users will actually log into, interact with, and rely on, WeWeb gives you a faster way to get there. See what others built with WeWeb Soraia : replaced Excel-heavy recruitment workflows with a custom platform built with WeWeb and Xano. Appy Makers : replaced a pathology lab’s manual slide archiving process with a mission-critical app built with WeWeb and Xano. PwC : built secure, compliant applications faster for internal operations and client needs. Shunpo : built a high-performance live quiz app for TF1 using WeWeb and Supabase. FAQs Q: Do I need coding skills to use a web app builder? A: Not for a no code platform. They are designed for visual development using drag and drop interfaces. However, for more complex applications or customizations, some low code platforms might benefit from basic scripting knowledge. The goal of a modern web application builder is to empower non technical users as much as possible. Q: Can a web application builder scale for large numbers of users? A: Yes, but it depends on the platform. Reputable builders are built on scalable cloud infrastructure. For maximum scalability, look for a builder that is backend agnostic. This allows you to connect your visually built frontend to any scalable backend service of your choice, giving you unlimited potential for growth. Q: Are apps built with a web application builder secure? A: Yes. Leading platforms prioritize security. They handle things like SSL encryption, secure user authentication, and run on secure cloud infrastructure. It’s important to choose a provider with a strong security track record and to configure your application’s permissions correctly. Q: What’s the difference between a web app builder and a website builder? A: Website builders (like Squarespace or Wix) are optimized for creating content based sites like blogs and portfolios. A web application builder is designed for creating interactive, data driven software with custom logic, user accounts, and database functionality, like a custom CRM or a project management tool. Q: What if I outgrow the web app builder? A: This is a valid concern, which is why avoiding vendor lock in is so important. The best platforms offer an escape hatch. Look for a builder that allows you to export your code or, even better, gives you the option to self host the application. This ensures you always own your product and can move it to your own infrastructure if needed. Platforms like WeWeb are designed with this freedom in mind.

title: Founder's Story: Bryn Jones
summary: CEO and Co-Founder Bryn Jones shares how PartnerStack came to be.
body_text: Would you believe that PartnerStack started out as a pretty bad version of Slack just 4 years ago? Let me take a step back and start at the beginning. My background I was a competitive swimmer growing up (yes, the very beginning - I promise it’ll be quick) and swam at international meets around the world from 2009-2011. In 2010 I got sick with what turned out to be swine flu, immediately followed by pneumonia. It was brutal and I had to take time off swimming. Feeling out of shape, I joined an intensive training camp at altitude in Arizona that ultimately pushed my body to the limit when I wasn’t in peak shape and caused my organs to swell. It was pretty detrimental and my body was never the same after. I finished my varsity year of swimming and was voted male athlete of the year, but that was the end of my competitive swimming career. That competitive spirit never left me, however, and it’s how I ended up at Western learning how athletes transition out of swimming into careers. And with the extra 30 hours I had back each week now that I wasn’t swimming, I had the time and energy to dedicate to a new pet project. PartnerStack’s 4 co-founders came together in 2014. Luke Swanek and I had been friends for 7 years when we met our other co-founders, Neil Chudleigh and Jon Mendes in grad school at Western. We were all in a business accelerator program there where we started working on a company we called Pod. Our first (horrible) startup was born It was essentially Slack for nonprofits. Neil and I even dropped out of school - against our families’ wishes of course - to dedicate our full attention to the fledgeling business. The 4 of us moved back to Toronto and lived together in a small house in Koreatown that we worked out of. Things were bad - Luke and I both took out loans and the debt started piling up; we couldn’t even afford a metro pass to get around the city for investor and sales meetings. We were driving a small amount of growing revenue but we couldn’t raise any capital and had no customers. Why? Because honestly we were a bad version of Slack . Potential customers kept asking us if Pod could do everything Slack does and we had to say it couldn't... We started paying outside people commissions to sell Pod for us, and through agencies in Toronto and London we started making 20K/month. We did realize it at first, but we’d basically created a channel marketing program. What helped me see the value of what we’d accidentally built was when companies started asking us how we were running our channel marketing. Our second startup was born At the end of 2014, I was in the air on my way to our holiday vacation when I realized Pod was a slow-moving business while we’d always wanted to create something high growth. After the holidays, I measured the opportunity cost of pursuing this vs. starting something new, and I somehow managed to convince my co-founders to build a landing page that focused on the one part of Pod that was working. It didn’t actually do anything at first but we talked about letting anyone refer a business and be rewarded. We even listed 10 ‘sample’ profiles of companies supposedly running channel programs through us (Including, of course, Microsoft among other big names). Then Luke and I started cold calling companies we thought had partner marketing programs and suggesting they use us. We landed 40 companies in 2 weeks and that was the proof we all needed to be sure we were onto something big. I did some serious research and learned that approximately $300 billion was sold yearly in SaaS, and that ⅓ is through 3rd party vendors - aka partners - but manually. Partner marketing was the last fossil in tech even though it was such a big revenue driver. Even as a manual process, it was a significant differentiator for the big companies like Microsoft, Cisco, Shopify, Hubspot, etc. who were already doing it and I was confident this was the direction we should be heading in. I think our perseverance was due in part to desperation - we needed this startup to work . Coming from Western University (not the more prestigious University of Waterloo), the 4 of us didn’t have an open door into the big tech companies. We applied to every incubator program we could find from 500 Startups to Techstars and beyond but no one was accepting us. We even drove to Philly during a nor'easter to interview at an incubator. The turning point We applied to Y Combinator (a leading accelerator program) 3 months after having the idea for PartnerStack (initially called GrowSumo based on a 5 minute search of cheap domain names); our site still didn’t work when we applied but we had a strong understanding of the issue companies were facing through our customer conversations. We were thrilled when they asked us to fly to California for an interview. As typical Canadians, we arrived in San Francisco and froze in our tee-shirts and shorts, but we all thought the interview went really well and were expecting to be accepted into the program. After a stressful night of checking our phones every hour, we finally got our acceptance call from Y Combinator’s Kevin Hale at 10:45pm, a few hours after we’d given up hope. We worked extremely hard during our time at Y Combinator and while we weren’t always impressing our advisors, we left as a top voted product on ProductHunt. This drove a ton of new customers for us and helped us close a round of funding in February 2016 before heading back home to Canada. The rest of that year we spent slowly and deliberately building a product that worked, and that customers wanted (this is Y Combinator’s mission too), with a very lean budget and team. We hired our first sales rep in 2017 and spent that year learning how to sell PartnerStack. 2018 has been spent scaling PartnerStack to the high growth company it is today (hooray!), but I think it’s the highs and lows along the way that really helped shape PartnerStack - and I'm grateful for all of the learning experiences we've had along the way.
